    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18874v1</id>
    <title>ChunkAct: Action Chunking for Agentic Robotics</title>
    <updated>2026-10-13T17:59:57Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18874v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18874v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Agentic robotics places a large language model (LLM) agent in the robot control loop, where it composes perception, motion, and vision-language-action (VLA) tools under the guidance of a memory and thereby generalizes to new tasks without retraining. This generality comes at a steep price in efficiency. Every primitive requires a round of LLM reasoning over the full interaction history, so the cost of an episode grows with the number of primitives. We find this reasoning largely redundant: once a sub-goal is chosen, its primitives follow a routine already prescribed by memory. We present ChunkAct, which introduces action chunking to agentic robotics. Online, a single call launches a chunk of chained primitives, which executes autonomously and returns control only upon failure. Offline, ChunkAct compiles the memory into these chunks, so execution is memory-free at test time and the planner is reserved for decisions that require reasoning. LLM computation therefore scales with the number of decisions rather than the number of primitives. On LIBERO-Pro, ChunkAct improves task success by 5.0 points over the state of the art in agentic robotics while requiring 2.9x fewer LLM calls, 4.4x fewer input tokens, and 2.3x fewer output tokens.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18871v1</id>
    <title>Cepheid: Decoupling Scale from Structure for Cross-Family Motion Completion</title>
    <updated>2026-10-13T17:59:53Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18871v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18871v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Sparse-to-dense motion completion recovers dense mesh motion from sparse vertex displacements. Residual priors trained on one geometry family frequently fail to beat parameter-free harmonic extension off-family. Moreover, cross-family training meets a scaling barrier: residual amplitude varies by more than an order of magnitude across geometry families and collapses as observations become denser. Since this scale depends on unknown target motion, it cannot be measured directly at test time. We decouple residual structure from physical scale by learning a dimensionless prior, estimating amplitude from observables and a lightweight correction fitted only on training sources. Our unified model surpasses harmonic extension across all evaluated families, including unseen cloth and legged bodies, without skeletons, registration, or cross-mesh correspondence. The same prior applies without retraining to point-tracked animal video and a robot grasping a soft body. Project page: https://su-terry.github.io/cepheid-website/</summary>

    <title>What Matters in Quality-Aware VLA Pretraining: A Benchmark and Empirical Study</title>
    <updated>2026-10-13T17:59:52Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18869v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18869v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>How should demonstration quality be used during vision-language-action (VLA) pretraining to improve performance after target-task fine-tuning? We compare weighting, filtering, and conditioning across reward definitions and label granularities using 5,000 naturally suboptimal human demonstrations and 24 target tasks. Within each VLA, we match demonstrations and training budgets. Additional comparisons examine pretraining data size and the roles of quality tags during fine-tuning and inference. Across three VLAs, we find that approach-aware episode conditioning improves mean success over plain behavioral cloning; conditioning and filtering favor episode and chunk labels, respectively, on average, with model-dependent reversals; and constant-tag fine-tuning improves mean success after conditioned pretraining with either tagged or untagged inference. We introduce AXIS-Bench to support these controlled comparisons. Built on crowdsourced simulation demonstrations, it provides recorded object and contact states for recomputing quality labels on shared trajectories. Replayable trajectories support workspace-aligned rendering and user-defined real-world target tasks. In our real-world experiment, simulation pretraining raises success from 9.6\% to 31.7\%. Project page: https://axis-bench.github.io/.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18868v1</id>
    <title>Tev: Scaling Long-Horizon Agentic Environments with Dense Progress Rewards</title>
    <updated>2026-10-13T17:59:51Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18868v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18868v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Long-horizon agents have drawn growing attention for their ability to work autonomously -- from hours to days -- on economically valuable tasks, a capability essential to automated discovery and recursive self-improvement (RSI). Yet open-source models still struggle on long-horizon tasks, largely for lack of both training data and a working recipe, and scaling both is hard: long, complex tasks are difficult to curate and verify, and their rewards are sparse. We address both. First, we introduce Tev-Gym, the first long-horizon agent training dataset with verifiable, dense, progressive rewards -- 1,170 verified task environments across 7 domains. It is built on a latent-world-first approach that first constructs a latent world: a complete and correct hidden specification of the task domain, workflow, and expected state after each step. Each task is then progressively rendered from this specification into an agent-facing environment, enabling controllable complexity and a natural progress metric. Second, we turn this metric into a training recipe: via progress-potential reward shaping (PPRS), we convert progress into a dense per-step reward that improves training efficiency and makes otherwise-intractable tasks trainable. Training with this recipe yields Tev-27B, which achieves substantial gains on the Agents' Last Exam computing and math sciences domains (ALE-CM), matching GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5 at Pass@5. Despite training only on ALE-related data, it generalizes to the Terminal-Bench (TB) 3.0 and 4.0 subsets, surpassing GLM 5.2 and Gemini 3.7 Flash, and reaches Claude Opus 4.8-level performance on middle-horizon tasks such as TB 2.1.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18863v1</id>
    <title>Data Free Training of Diffusion Models for Lattice Field Theories</title>
    <updated>2026-10-13T17:59:33Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18863v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18863v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Sampling equilibrium field configurations remains a major computational bottleneck in lattice field theory, motivating the development of generative samplers that can produce independent configurations. Diffusion models are promising for this purpose, but their standard denoising score matching objective requires samples from the target distribution, seemingly reintroducing the original sampling problem. Here, we show that diffusion models can instead be trained from their own generated samples using the target score identity, provided access to the unnormalized probability density. Importance-weighted formulations of this identity yield a consistent target throughout training, while unweighted variants define a self-consistent fixed-point training scheme. We benchmark the different approaches in two-dimensional \(φ^4\) theory and identify effective choices that enable efficient training and sampling across the symmetric, critical, and broken phases. Ultimately, our data-free training approach achieves comparable performance to training on HMC reference data.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18862v1</id>
    <title>DoubtLess: Training-Free Contrastive Decoding for Efficient Reasoning</title>
    <updated>2026-10-13T17:59:32Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18862v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18862v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Reasoning models achieve strong performance through long chains of thought (CoT), but often spend more tokens than needed to solve a problem. Existing ways to shorten the CoT require additional training for each model, add a fixed steering vector to the model's hidden states, or use decoding heuristics such as stopping early or banning words like "wait", which can reduce accuracy. We propose DoubtLess, a training-free decoding method in which a much smaller reasoning model steers the large one towards brevity. The small model reads the large model's CoT so far twice, once prompted to be brief (the brief thinker) and once prompted to be verbose (the verbose thinker), and the difference between its two logit vectors, scaled by a strength, is added to the large model's logits at every step of the CoT. On seven benchmarks of competition mathematics, graduate-level science and competitive programming, DoubtLess shortens the CoT of Qwen3-32B by 31% with unchanged accuracy, outperforming five inference-time baselines. We also show that DoubtLess reduces thinking tokens per turn by 20% in a self-debugging coding agent with unchanged task performance. It also generalizes to two other model families with unchanged accuracy. When combined with training-based compression, it further shortens the CoT of a model already trained for brevity. Ablations and behavioral analysis show that DoubtLess reduces repeated checking, with most token savings coming after the correct answer first appears in the CoT. Our code is available at https://github.com/leoluolol/DoubtLess.</summary>

    <title>AesCode: Aesthetic Code Generation with Decoupled Cross-Modal Rewards</title>
    <updated>2026-10-13T17:59:31Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18860v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18860v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Generating information-rich visual artifacts such as slides, posters, and dashboards as code is appealing because the outputs are structured, editable, and verifiable. Yet code models cannot see how their choices of layout and color come together on the canvas, often limiting spatial planning and aesthetic quality. Image generators excel at visual design but can misrender requested content, making their outputs unreliable targets for direct reproduction. We therefore introduce AesCode, which generates code grounded in the content prompt while using an image generated from the same prompt as an aesthetic guidance. To do so, AesCode represents the target as a design graph that describes the whole canvas and makes each property attributable. From this graph, we derive complementary cross-modal rewards: deterministic verifiers score properties parsable from code and rendering, while a VLM judge assesses the non-parsable ones with a sample-specific Visual Graph Rubric (VGR) tied to graph elements and relations. We optimize these decoupled rewards through reinforcement learning with per-channel normalization to jointly improve spatial planning, aesthetic quality, and verifiable correctness. To evaluate this setting, we build a benchmark that scores verifiable correctness and visual quality separately, with visual scores highly consistent with human judgments. We find that reference images substantially improve the visual quality of code generated by existing models, and ablations show that AesCode benefits from references both as model input and as a source of visual rewards. Relative to same-scale Qwen3-VL baselines given the same references, AesCode-8B and AesCode-32B improve visual quality by 31.1 and 22.4 percentage points, reaching scores comparable to those of closed-source frontier models such as GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18861v1</id>
    <title>Hybrid Reasoning Agents</title>
    <updated>2026-10-13T17:59:31Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18861v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18861v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>How can we build an agent that thinks beyond human language, yet still acts through it in the external environment? Modern LLM agents still reason and interact through text, while latent reasoning offers an efficient internal medium but lacks native tool access and reasoning transparency. We bridge these two directions with Hybrid Reasoning Agents (HybridAgents), which dynamically navigate between latent reasoning and text-based interaction throughout a unified generation process. Architecturally, a lightweight HybridLink enables seamless transitions between text and latent modes, while the agent's continuous working memory preserves lossless hybrid context across multiple turns. These designs preserve tool-integrated agentic capabilities while making latent thoughts directly inspectable. Building on this architecture, we further develop dedicated post-training algorithms for hybrid reasoning: HybridSFT stabilizes tool-integrated hybrid generation by teaching the backbone to coordinate with HybridLink, then HybridRL scales reasoning by learning when to think in latent space and when to act through text. We evaluate HybridAgent at 3 model scales across 11 benchmarks covering mathematics, science, medicine, search, and agentic reasoning. Compared with frontier LLM Agents and agentic frameworks spanning both text-based and latent methods, HybridAgent consistently improves performance by 10.4%, while delivering 35.5%-54.7% token reduction, 1.8x-2.6x faster inference, and 2.7x-3.7x cost savings. Code and data are available at https://github.com/togethercomputer/HybridAgent.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18856v1</id>
    <title>Exact Topological Compliance: Generating Persistence-Equivalent Graphs</title>
    <updated>2026-10-13T17:59:19Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18856v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18856v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Persistent homology summarizes the topological evolution of a graph as persistence diagrams (PDs). Generating graphs whose topology matches a target descriptor is increasingly important, yet existing topology-aware generative models rely on soft regularization, producing graphs whose PDs may only be approximately similar. We initiate a principled investigation of the generation problem: produce graphs that realize a target PD exactly. We propose two approaches guided by the implicit local and global constraints a target PD imposes. The local approach builds degree-based PD-equivalent graphs iteratively, and we prove that every output realizes the target PD and that every degree-based PD-equivalent graph is reachable. However, as shown thereafter, local generation necessarily trades off between sample diversity and reaching infeasible states. We therefore recast generation as a global constraint satisfaction problem with a complete encoding solvable by modern constraint programming solvers. This is applicable to any vertex-based permutation equivariant filtration scheme and is minimal under the degree filtration. Experiments on four standard graph generation benchmarks confirm that both methods realize the target PD exactly. Together, our methods provide a principled treatment of strict topology-compliant graph generation. Code is available at https://github.com/Aalto-QuML/ExactCompliance.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18853v1</id>
    <title>Two Clocks: Why Larger Rollout Batches Learn Slower but Fail on Schedule in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards</title>
    <updated>2026-10-13T17:58:57Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18853v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18853v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) relies on costly model-generated responses, motivating larger rollout batches and square-root learning-rate scaling. Reported to approximately preserve progress per sample with one optimizer step per rollout, this rule is less understood in practical multi-step training. We develop a two-clock framework that separates the samples needed to make progress from those consumed before collapse. Under a local quadratic model, the square-root rule preserves first-order drift per sample but not progress: larger batches take fewer, longer updates and lose more to curvature, yielding a learning-rate-dependent critical batch beyond which sample efficiency degrades. A drift-threshold hypothesis predicts a complementary failure clock whose sample count remains approximately invariant along the square-root rule. Controlled GRPO experiments on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B across a $16\times$ batch range support both predictions. Ratio clipping delays failure, especially for larger batches, but the progress gap persists without it. Widening the clip trades stability for a transient speed gain. The progress gap reappears on another dataset, a general-purpose checkpoint, and a 7B model. Finally, we use the two-clock framework to derive a simple multi-step RLVR schedule: start below the critical batch and switch to a larger batch before failure. Our code is available at: https://github.com/WinstonLiyt/two-clocks-rlvr.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18851v1</id>
    <title>MFG: Multi-turn Feedback Guided Molecular Optimization</title>
    <updated>2026-10-13T17:58:41Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18851v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18851v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Multi-objective molecular optimization is a critical process in drug discovery that aims to modify a given molecule to simultaneously improve multiple properties while maintaining a similar overall structure. This process often requires iterative modifications guided by computational or experimental feedback. Recent large language model (LLM)-based methods have begun to explore this iterative approach; however, these methods are not explicitly trained to leverage such feedback, while existing approaches primarily focus on single-turn molecular optimization. To address this gap, we introduce Multi-turn Feedback Guided (MFG) molecular optimization, a reinforcement learning framework that trains an LLM to progressively optimize molecules using feedback from previous turns. MFG introduces a feedback vector capturing both property improvements and source molecule similarity, alongside a feedback-aligned reward function that promotes progressive improvement across turns. We apply MFG over $\text{GeLLM}^{3}\text{O}$, a state-of-the-art LLM model for multi-objective molecular optimization, evaluate $\text{GeLLM}^{3}\text{O-MFG}$ on ten multi-objective molecular optimization tasks. The results demonstrate that $\text{GeLLM}^{3}\text{O-MFG}$ achieves the highest average similarity-constrained success rate ($81.50%$), outperforming the base model $\text{GeLLM}^{3}\text{O}$ ($70.81%$).</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18843v1</id>
    <title>LIBERO-RIG: A Hardware-Setup Robustness Benchmark for Vision-Language-Action Models</title>
    <updated>2026-10-13T17:57:18Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18843v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18843v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Robot policies are expected to generalize across deployment environments, including variations in the robot itself: cameras are bumped and remounted, calibrations drift, controllers run at different rates, and end-effector pads wear down. We present LIBERO-RIG, a benchmark that perturbs only the robot's hardware and setup while holding every LIBERO task fixed. The benchmark spans eleven perturbation axes, including camera mounting and optics, camera-to-arm calibration, actuation gain, control rate, proprioceptive noise, base pose, table height, and gripper pads. Each axis has five severity levels, yielding 210 conditions across the four LIBERO suites. We evaluate nine recent vision-language-action models using 500 episodes per condition and substantiate each finding with rigorous statistical tests. Pooled success falls from 0.932 to 0.767 at the middle severity and 0.509 at the highest severity. Performance degradation varies substantially across perturbation axes and action interfaces, and training on visual perturbations does not mitigate faults that leave camera images unchanged. We release the benchmark together with manifests specifying the fixed perturbation parameters for each episode.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18842v1</id>
    <title>Who Improves the Robot? Toward Physical Recursive Self-Improvement</title>
    <updated>2026-10-13T17:57:04Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18842v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18842v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Robots are increasingly autonomous in task execution, yet their improvement remains largely human-driven. This study investigates Physical Recursive Self-Improvement (Physical RSI), in which physical experience guides lasting updates to both a robot's capabilities and its improvement procedure, making subsequent improvement more effective across tasks. Physical RSI faces challenges from noisy observations, continuous dynamics, costly trials, and irreversible consequences. We present an L0-L5 framework that differentiates capability-level from meta-level updates and within-task from across-task gains, reserving L5 for independently verified recursive gain. We study existing methods around harness adaptation and model training, alongside safety and control mechanisms that govern execution and successive updates. Our analysis reveals that, despite substantial progress in self-improvement, the surveyed literature does not yet demonstrate Physical RSI as defined by our framework. We identify research priorities in reliable feedback, causal attribution, safety preservation, and benchmarking, outlining a path toward robots that autonomously improve how they learn while ensuring safety. The GitHub repository for Physical RSI is available at https://github.com/SAIL-Research-Lab/Physical-RSI.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18839v1</id>
    <title>Fast Rates for Offline Q-Learning with KL Regularization</title>
    <updated>2026-10-13T17:56:27Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18839v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18839v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>This paper investigates offline Q-learning for finite-horizon Markov decision processes with Kullback-Leibler (KL) regularization. Recent studies have shown that KL regularization can yield fast rates in offline decision-making problems. However, it remains unclear whether Q-learning, which adopts incremental stochastic approximation updates, can achieve such fast rates in the offline setting. We first propose KL-regularized Q-Learning (KLQ), a simple variant of classical Q-learning. By exploiting KL regularization, we prove that KLQ achieves a sample complexity of $\widetilde{O}(1/ε)$ without explicit pessimism. This guarantee, however, has an exponential dependence on the KL regularization parameter and the horizon. To address this limitation, we further propose KL-regularized Pessimistic Q-Learning (KLPQ), which incorporates pessimism into KLQ. We prove that KLPQ retains the same \(\widetilde O(1/ε)\) rate while removing the explicit exponential dependence, thereby further improving the sample complexity. To the best of our knowledge, these results establish the first fast-rate guarantees for offline Q-learning in tabular finite-horizon KL-regularized MDPs.</summary>

    <title>Scaling Online Optimal Transport Minibatches for Flow Matching</title>
    <updated>2026-10-13T17:56:26Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18838v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18838v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>A central challenge in scaling flow models is maintaining stability in training and integration. In flow matching, this stability depends critically on how source samples are paired with data. Independent random pairing introduces substantial stochasticity, motivating minibatch optimal transport (OT) to construct online source-target couplings that reduce this randomness (Tong et al., 2024). However, as applications extend to larger and higher-dimensional datasets, small minibatches can limit these benefits, while scaling the coupling to substantially larger minibatches at every iteration is computationally prohibitive. Moreover, how OT coupling affects the full stochastic gradient and integration remains theoretically unresolved. In this work, we develop a scalable online entropic OT approximation that enables substantially larger source-target couplings while preserving the benefits of OT. We close the theoretical gap for both unregularized and entropic OT by proving strict reductions in full stochastic-gradient variance and integration error relative to independent pairing, and further characterize how these improvements strengthen as the online coupling minibatch grows. Experiments on single-cell gene interpolation-flow and image-flow training validate these predictions, showing that larger online couplings consistently improve training stability and final generation performance.</summary>

    <summary>It is difficult to accurately model the physics of the interaction between a robot and the objects it manipulates, including contact mechanics, coupled contact dynamics, deformations, stiffness and friction.     <title>Gaussian entanglement and quantum communication: geodesic optimization and multimode bounds</title>
    <updated>2026-10-13T17:53:59Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18827v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18827v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Loss and noise limit the use of light to distribute entanglement, transmit quantum information, and establish secret keys. Gaussian states have a compact description in terms of means and covariance matrices, but their entanglement still requires global optimization. We develop a framework for computing Gaussian-restricted versions of the relative entropy of entanglement and Rains entanglement. An integral representation reveals a convex geometry under matrix geometric means and reduces Gaussian Rains entanglement to relative entropy minimized over Gaussian states with positive partial transpose. We obtain unique optimal reference states and additivity for independent Gaussian input states. Our convex-majorization algorithm has an explicit geometric convergence rate, uniform in the faithful regularization parameter and valid for pure input states. Controlled numerical integration and approximate convex subproblem solutions give a bit-complexity bound that is polynomial in accuracy bits for each fixed rational input covariance matrix, with explicit dependence on covariance size. These calculations bound extractable entanglement and, through the relative entropy of entanglement, extractable secret key. Teleportation simulation, energy allocation, and a convex optimization of passive-basis loss cores give bounds on quantum and private communication under an input-energy constraint, allowing arbitrary two-way classically assisted protocols. Two- and three-mode examples compare the bounds with achievable rates, including matching pure-loss benchmarks.     <title>Joint Neural Posterior Estimation and Model Selection for Chemical Reaction Networks</title>
    <updated>2026-10-13T17:52:39Z</updated>

    <summary>Simulation-based Bayesian inference for Chemical Reaction Networks (CRNs) must simultaneously solve two computationally demanding problems: discriminating between overlapping reaction pathways and estimating reaction rate constants. Classical approaches, such as Sequential Monte Carlo ABC, rely on handcrafted summary statistics and scale poorly across large parameter spaces.     <title>Read the Room Before Your Model Generates</title>
    <updated>2026-10-13T17:51:18Z</updated>

    <summary>Large language models (LLMs) generally rely on sampling temperature to regulate the amount of randomness in their outputs. Mainstream methods for selecting temperature typically involve fixed, heuristic global settings and context or token-level calibration, rather than a geometrically interpretable representation of the communicative scenario. Scenario-Actor extracts scenario-relevant structures from Transformer hidden states and determines the temperature from scenario embedding, a structured geometric representation of the communicative setting. Empirical results show that on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Scenario-Actor achieves strong goal-completion performance in interactive social scenarios, significant gains on open-ended instruction following, and competitive performance on multi-turn conversation compared to multiple baselines.</summary>

    <title>Back-Translation Still Matters: Leveraging Monolingual Data for Low-Resource Machine Translation with LLMs</title>
    <updated>2026-10-13T17:50:18Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18818v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18818v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Pre-trained Large Language Model (LLMs) are effective on many tasks in zero-shot and few-shot settings. For machine translation of low-resource languages, the obvious options are few-shot prompting and fine-tuning on a small parallel set. We ask: what if moderate amounts of low-resource monolingual data are also available? We argue that, rather than continued pretraining, a more effective use of this data is the pre-LLM era technique of back-translation (BT). The current fine-tuned LLM translates monolingual sentences in each language, and the resulting pairs train it in the reverse direction. Updates on the parallel set are interleaved for stable learning. With 1K parallel pairs on Odia and Swahili, BT beats continued pretraining into the low-resource language by 7.7 to 16.4 XCOMET-XXL points in domain. With beam-decoded intermediate translations, it also beats a model with 10 time more parallel data. In-context examples retrieved from the parallel data further improve BT. We also analyze the source, quality and amount of monolingual text. Across five low-resource languages, with Hindi as a high-resource control, and two 3B backbones, BT improves translation into the low-resource language by 16 to 173% XCOMET-XXL over parallel-only fine-tuning. Blind human evaluation on Odia and Sanskrit agrees with the automatic metrics.</summary>

    <title>On the coincidence of discrete and continuous definitions of Entanglement of Formation</title>
    <updated>2026-10-13T17:49:45Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18816v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18816v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>It is proved that every Borel ensemble of pure states on a separable bipartite Hilbert space with finite average entanglement admits a countable ensemble with the same barycenter and arbitrarily small additional average entanglement. Consequently, the discrete and continuous versions of the Entanglement of Formation coincide on the whole space of states of infinite-dimensional bipartite quantum system (with infinite values allowed).
  The main idea of the proof (realized with the AI-assistance) is the identification of a Borel ensemble of pure bipartite states with a Borel probability measure on the unit sphere of the space of Hilbert--Schmidt operators followed by dividing the support of this measure into appropriate cells and replacing each cell by its conditional barycenter. The resulting countable ensemble is obtained by a recursive construction.</summary>

    <title>Self-Evolving Agent Harness</title>
    <updated>2026-10-13T17:48:49Z</updated>

    <summary>Harness self-evolution revises an agent's software scaffolding, including prompts, memory, workflows, and executable components, while keeping model weights fixed. We formalize a feedback-driven process in which accepted revisions persist across runs. The framework separates update targets from proposal and admission mechanisms. It distinguishes changes to interpreted state from revisions to tools and code, repository-level control logic, and plugin composition. We characterize search through evolutionary optimization and examine its reliability through continual PAC-learning. Under explicit assumptions, the analysis yields an expected generalization bound, a retention bound conditional on historical regression budgets, and a high-probability admission rule using fresh, independent validation data. We examine how persistent harness revisions affect knowledge sharing and organizational workflows, with implications for scientific reliability, physical safety, and institutional accountability. Cases from prior work illustrate model--harness co-design, distributed execution, and plugin reuse. Reliable deployment requires continual validation as task distributions and evaluators change, with independent safeguards for learning, runtime privileges, and consequential actions. We provide a comprehensive 66-page discussion of related work, theory, algorithms, evaluation, applications, and the broader impact of Harness RSI, together with continuously updated code and supplementary materials, at https://github.com/zgcagi/Harness-RSI.</summary>

    <title>Statistical Vignettes on the Grokking Phenomenon</title>
    <updated>2026-10-13T17:47:56Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18811v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18811v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>In this work, we study grokking in a simple, analytically tractable setting whose rich phenomenology allows us to disentangle the effects of initialization, signal strength, weight decay, sample size, and input dimension. These factors can produce superficially similar learning curves through distinct mechanisms, complicating their interpretation. Our analysis distinguishes early fitting through nuisance features, core feature learning, and delayed generalization. We identify sharp conditions under which grokking provably occurs and derive analytic asymptotic expressions for the lengths of the generalization plateaus. Our results also characterize regimes of early generalization and failure to reach a prescribed test accuracy target. We show that the interpolation edge constitutes a distinct dynamical regime, where vanishing spectral gaps separate core learning from generalization, helping clarify the role of proximity to interpolation in existing accounts of grokking. The resulting picture is analogous to fast and slow phases in chemical kinetics and suggests that the lazy-to-rich transition discussed in the literature may reflect a similar separation of dynamical time scales. Our theoretical results are faithfully supported by extensive experiments.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18809v1</id>
    <title>Depth Memory</title>
    <updated>2026-10-13T17:46:33Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18809v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18809v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Residual connections propagate information through a network by additively accumulating layer outputs. Recently proposed alternatives, such as Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) and Attention Residuals (AttnRes), instead use more expressive depth aggregation mechanisms that improve language modeling performance at scale. In this work, we consider the mixing of representations over depth as a problem of storing and retrieving information across layers. Formalizing this perspective, we introduce Depth Memory (DM), a unified framework that describes the standard pre-layer-norm (PreLN) transformer, mHC, and AttnRes in terms of streams that carry representations through the network. One such stream, for example, could be an explicit memory stream that is queried to enrich the input to every layer, and whose output is subsequently written back into the memory for use by later layers. For AttnRes, this memory stream is a growing cache of explicit layer representations. For mHC, it is an expanded residual stream. Building on this view, we propose Linear Depth Memory (LDM), which formulates information retrieval across depth as a regression problem solved using recursive least squares. The resulting architecture propagates three streams across depth: the standard residual stream, a linear associative memory stream, and an inverse covariance stream. For high-throughput training and inference, we propose a hardware-aware implementation of LDM that reduces peak activation memory and memory traffic. LDM consistently achieves the lowest perplexities among PreLN, mHC and AttnRes baselines at the 400M and 1.5B parameter scales, alongside competitive zero-shot accuracy.</summary>

    <title>Optimizing Team Behavior via Extremum-seeking Control in Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning</title>
    <updated>2026-10-13T17:46:27Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18808v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>

    <summary>In cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL), agents must learn to coordinate their actions to achieve shared objectives. A key indicator of effective coordination is behavioral diversity, i.e., the agents' potential to enact distinct yet complementary control policies given the same set of observations. Although behavioral diversity can enable role specialization and richer joint behaviors, its appropriate level is highly context- and task-dependent and often costly to tune. We propose Adaptive Diversity Control (ADiCo), a two-timescale framework that adapts behavioral diversity online during training. On a fast timescale, Diversity Control (DiCo) regulates system diversity toward a target value. On a slower timescale, an Extremum Seeking Controller (ESC) adjusts this target using only mean episodic returns, without requiring an explicit model or analytical gradient of the diversity-performance landscape. We evaluate ADiCo on six configurations across two cooperative MARL tasks, where it maintains task-appropriate diversity levels: low diversity when homogeneous policies are beneficial and higher diversity when heterogeneous policies are required. Through this adaptation, ADiCo matches or exceeds the mean performance of DiCo (best grid-searched diversity target) and Unconstrained DiCo (diversity allowed to emerge without target regulation). These results demonstrate that incorporating classical feedback control into MARL training enables effective coordination by providing a systematic alternative to task-specific manual selection of the diversity target.</summary>

    <title>SkillScaffold: Scaffolding Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Policy-Adaptive Skill Credit Assignment and Selective Injection</title>
    <updated>2026-10-13T17:46:25Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18807v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>

    <summary>Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) enables large language models (LLMs) to learn from multi-turn interactions with verifiable outcomes. Textual skills can improve exploration by distilling prior interactions into reusable guidance. However, existing skill-based RL approaches often either assume skill injection is beneficial or rely on indirect feedback or rollout-intensive evaluation to assess its utility. Our pilot studies show that rollout-based utility estimation for skill credit assignment is costly and unstable under limited sampling, while skill benefits vary across candidates and depend on the current policy's competence on each query. To address these challenges, we introduce SkillScaffold, a policy-adaptive training scaffold that combines low-cost skill-utility estimation with selective skill injection. By reusing outcome-verified training trajectories, SkillScaffold generates candidate skills and estimates their utility through outcome-aware likelihood comparisons, without candidate-specific environment rollouts. The resulting utility guides whether and which skill to inject, retaining skill-free execution when no candidate is estimated to help. Joint training enables the Generator to produce skills tailored to the evolving Executor. Scaffolded RL encourages skill internalization for skill-free inference. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, ScienceWorld, and $τ^2$-Bench demonstrate gains over strong agentic-RL and skill-based RL baselines across both short- and long-horizon tasks. Ablations and further analyses support the importance of utility-based selection and abstention. Our code is available at https://github.com/Vaidurya00/SkillScaffold.</summary>

    <title>Registration is a Representation Problem: Solving Whole-Body PET/CT Registration</title>
    <updated>2026-10-13T17:45:34Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18804v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>

    <summary>Raw image intensities are a poor surrogate for similarity across images in correspondence problems. Further, while auxiliary segmentation labels can provide semantic identification and improve matching, they can assign only coarse identities to fine-grained anatomy and often cover only a subset of structures, particularly in whole-body settings. We present an approach that instead establishes correspondence using complementary representations of anatomy and demonstrate its utility for longitudinal whole-body PET/CT registration in the Learn2Reg 2026 PSMAReg Challenge. Our 3D foundation model, anatomix, is used to derive fine-grained, per-voxel semantic representations that are consistent across volumes, and we further employ off-the-shelf segmentation models to obtain coarse anatomical identities. Together, these representations drive a GPU-accelerated iterative registration solver (FireANTs) in a hybrid multistage framework: the first stage estimates alignment from dense multi-channel features, after which a second refines the deformation using both anatomix- and segmentation-based losses. Lastly, because registration should not introduce non-biological tumor volume changes across time, we develop lesion-specific component-wise volume preservation schemes. Without any task-specific training, our system won first place in the PSMAReg Challenge leaderboard. Code and interactive visualizations are available at http://www.neeldey.com/reps-for-reg.</summary>

    <title>$\mathsf{EFI}\Leftrightarrow\mathsf{1PRS}$</title>
    <updated>2026-10-13T17:42:13Z</updated>

    <summary>A series of recent works has established EFI pairs as the "minimal" assumption for quantum cryptography. Recently, Cavalar et al. [CCC+26] showed that EFI pairs are equivalent to non-uniform expanding single-copy pseudorandom state generators (1PRS), and obtained a non-uniform meta-complexity characterization of EFI pairs. We remove the non-uniformity in their construction and prove that EFI pairs are equivalent to expanding 1PRS. As a corollary, we obtain the first uniform meta-complexity characterization of EFI pairs. Together with the equivalence of statistically verifiable one-way state generators and commitments proved by Batra and Jain [BJ24], this gives a quantum analogue of the classical equivalence between one-way functions, commitments, and pseudorandom generators.</summary>

    <title>SEAR: Self-Evolving Agentic Robotics</title>
    <updated>2026-10-13T17:40:20Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18792v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18792v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Frontier language-model agents can now improve robots on their own: they write control code, test it, and keep what works as skills and memories for the next task. We introduce SEAR (Self-Evolving Agentic Robotics), a framework and benchmark built around two questions. Is the agent really learning, or just trying more often? And does what it learns still help on new tasks, in a new simulator, and on a real robot? The framework runs an agent in three modes: it writes code that becomes the policy (code-as-policy), acts live in the control loop (agent-as-policy), or works as a researcher that fine-tunes a vision-language-action model (auto-research). The benchmark adds controls that separate retained experience from repeated attempts, familiar tasks, privileged simulator state, larger budgets, and luck. Across seven frontier language models, 330 simulated and five physical tasks, and over four years of agent runtime, we highlight three findings. First, the learning curve of a robotic agent depends both on the overall time budget and the task difficulty relative to model capability. Harder tasks make longer sessions worthwhile; on easier tasks, re-rolling short attempts does just as well. Second, control code and shared routines transfer across tasks and simulators, while task-specific solutions do not. On a real robot, we observe a performance gap between agent-designed practice and novel human-designed scenes. Third, different models evolve more effectively in different ways. Some do best acting live, others writing code first. And a text-only model keeps pace with a comparable multimodal one: perception helps with error assessment, but agentic reasoning and tool use can matter more. We release the benchmark and codebase to support future research.</summary>

    <summary>Existing malware detection approaches heavily rely on handcrafted features derived from static or dynamic analysis of the executable files. These methods require specialized domain expertise, dedicated analysis tools, and time-consuming analysis, which limits their scalability and robustness in the face of the increasing complexity and diversity of modern malware. Consequently, there is a growing interest in approaches that operate directly on raw bytes, which contain rich semantic and structural information. However, capturing long-range dependencies within executable files remains challenging for conventional static and CNN-based methods. This paper presents MalwareFormer, a transformer-based, byte-level malware detection framework that operates directly on raw bytes, without requiring domain knowledge or feature extraction. MalwareFormer achieves an accuracy of 98.35%, a balanced accuracy of 98.32%, a macro-F1 of 98.32%, and a false positive rate of 1.94%, outperforming both baselines across all threshold-dependent classification metrics and demonstrating that transformers provide a powerful and scalable approach for byte-level malware detection.</summary>

    <title>Where Do LLM Ensemble Gains Come From? Decomposing Candidate Value, Diversity, and Aggregation</title>
    <updated>2026-10-13T17:36:51Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18786v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18786v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>LLM ensemble gains are often measured against a single baseline, but the value attributed to additional candidates can change with the comparison used. We study an LLM aggregator under four matched conditions: Direct (no candidates), Single-slot (one candidate in a multi-slot interface), Duplicate (one candidate repeated), and Multi-candidate (separately generated candidates). Under either non-diverse control, overall candidate gain (CIV) splits algebraically into an additional-candidate contrast (DSV) and a candidate-context contrast (CCV); the split, but not CIV, depends on the chosen control. On MultiHopRAG model diversity (k=2), the repetition gap Rep=-8.33 pp [-13.25, -3.75] quantifies the difference between gains measured against Duplicate and Single-slot. On a matched FRAMES stronger-panel extension (n=200, k=3, aggregator output limit 4096), paired Delta Rep=+9.67 pp [+6.00, +13.50]; within panels, Rep changes sign (original -6.33; stronger +3.33). In FRAMES evidence aggregation, candidate-context contrasts remain strongly negative under both non-diverse controls. Our results show why ensemble evaluations should state the reference control before attributing gains to additional candidates.</summary>

    <title>Relative-Entropy Geometry and Convergence in Nonconvex Wiretap Optimization</title>
    <updated>2026-10-13T17:35:33Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18785v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18785v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We develop and analyze an entropic descent method for a nonconvex optimization problem on probability simplices arising in classical and quantum secure communication. The optimization variables describe a randomized encoder, allowing its input distribution and stochastic preprocessing to be optimized jointly. An exact relative-entropy identity yields a channel-independent majorization bound and an explicit mirror-descent iteration with a fixed unit step size. We establish quantitative descent, convergence of objective values, and stationarity of accumulation points on their support faces for arbitrary finite classical channels, without assuming degradedness or less noisiness. For strictly positive transition matrices, a square-root parametrization and a Kurdyka--Łojasiewicz argument establish finite length of the transformed trajectory and convergence of the entire sequence, including limits on the simplex boundary. For less-noisy channels, a restricted convex formulation admits global convergence with an explicit \(O(1/t)\) objective-error bound. We extend the relative-entropy construction to noncommuting quantum outputs and derive monotone alternating updates for covariant encoders, including correlated preprocessing over a fixed block. Numerical experiments compare the method with analytic benchmarks and constrained optimization, reveal multiple attracting values, and demonstrate strict improvements from stochastic preprocessing.</summary>

    <title>Pack Light, CarryOn: Building Object-Oriented Context for Long-Horizon Agents</title>
    <updated>2026-10-13T17:35:27Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18784v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18784v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Long-horizon agents accumulate progress in persistent task state, yet repeatedly process interaction histories describing how that progress was achieved. This raises a natural question: can long-horizon context instead be organized around reusable progress rather than the history that produced it? In this paper, we introduce CarryOn, an object-oriented context runtime that organizes continuation around reusable task objects. Rather than treating compressed histories or reconstructed accounts of progress as the primary basis for continuation, CarryOn builds a context view from continuation carriers, complementary execution context, and a live tail of recent interactions. A core challenge is keeping this reusable basis valid after its surrounding history is retired: how can CarryOn update the basis without reconstructing the full representation at every fold? CarryOn maintains carrier records across folds, revising affected records against bound evidence and applicable environment checks while carrying forward unaffected records and jointly updating execution context. Experiments on OSWorld 2.0 and BrowseComp-Plus show improved gains of 5.8% and 7.0% while reducing total token usage by 51.9% and 22.9%, respectively. Project page: https://ethannju.github.io/carryon</summary>

    <title>BLADE: Auditing Information Use for Failure Attribution in LLM Multi-Agent Systems</title>
    <updated>2026-10-13T17:34:34Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18780v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18780v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Large language model multi-agent systems extend individual agents' capabilities through collaboration across specialized roles, tools, and workflows. Yet collaboration makes failures harder to diagnose: one agent may misinterpret a correct result while others carry the mistake forward. Failure attribution therefore seeks to identify the responsible agent and decisive error step. Recent methods trace dependencies, but knowing where information came from is not the same as knowing where it went wrong. We introduce BLADE (Blame Localization via Audited Dependency Evidence), a training-free framework that moves beyond tracing information to auditing its use. Using Jev for structured probabilistic judgments, BLADE uses dependency probabilities to select relevant source-decision handoffs for auditing. At these handoffs, it examines whether receiving decisions use their sources faithfully and within task requirements, distinguishing error introduction, propagation, and repair. These findings inform a global diagnosis that considers all execution steps. Without reference answers, BLADE achieves the best or tied-best step accuracy among eight strategies under a shared Jev decision interface on 1,228 failed runs across five Who&When and Who&When Pro subsets, outperforming All-at-once by 2.2-11.1 percentage points. Making responsibility evidence explicit offers a path toward more interpretable and reliable agentic systems.</summary>

    <title>Deterministic and programmable generation of mechanical multipartite entangled states</title>
    <updated>2026-10-13T17:32:44Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18778v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18778v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Multimode mechanical resonators offer a large set of densely packed, long-lived bosonic modes within a single compact device, making them attractive for quantum simulation, quantum information processing, and quantum-enhanced sensing. Many such applications rely on multipartite entanglement, yet deterministic mechanical entanglement has so far been largely limited to pairs of modes. Here we demonstrate the deterministic and programmable preparation of multipartite entangled states among the phonon modes of a high-overtone bulk acoustic wave resonator coupled to a superconducting transmon qubit. By sequentially applying optimal-control-engineered isometries between the qubit and successive modes, we generate matrix product states of bond dimension two, including $W$, Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ), and cluster states. We fully characterize these states via quantum state tomography and certify genuine multipartite entanglement among up to four modes. We further demonstrate correlated-noise sensing by exploiting the complementary decoherence responses of the stored $W$ and GHZ states, isolating inter-mode phase correlations from local decoherence and placing quantitative bounds on collective dephasing. Our results establish a scalable approach to preparing multipartite entangled states in mechanical systems, with promising applications in multiparameter sensing and tests of quantum mechanics with massive objects.</summary>

    <title>Quantum-enhanced mechanical sensing with machine-learning estimation</title>
    <updated>2026-10-13T17:32:42Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18776v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18776v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Massive mechanical oscillators couple directly to forces, accelerations and gravity, making them attractive probes of new physics and of quantum mechanics at macroscopic scales. Pushing sensitivities beyond the standard quantum limit for signals of unknown phase requires non-Gaussian quantum states, whose metrological advantage has so far been confined to lighter systems such as trapped ions. Here we operate a microgram-scale acoustic mode of a high-overtone bulk acoustic wave resonator as a phase-insensitive quantum-enhanced sensor. A transmon qubit prepares the mode in Fock states of up to seven phonons by optimal control, and resolves its phonon-number distribution after interaction with a weak resonant signal. Bayesian analysis yields a Fisher information five times the vacuum value, a 7.0 dB gain in signal-amplitude sensitivity over any classical probe state, irrespective of its energy, currently limited by state preparation infidelities. We then train a neural network on the measured sensor response to perform Bayesian estimation without any analytical model of the system, showing the same sensitivity gain with half the systematic bias. Our results establish acoustic resonators prepared in non-Gaussian states as quantum-enhanced probes for high-frequency gravitational waves, dark matter and wave-function collapse.</summary>

    <title>Jeva: System One Models from First Principles</title>
    <updated>2026-10-13T17:31:09Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18773v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18773v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>System one models enable direct, low-latency decision-making. Yet recent practice of predicting an answer from serialized text does not, by itself, respect the structure of a decision problem. We argue that current designs underemphasize four important structural requirements. (i) null-aware: Models should distinguish answer absence from uncertainty among candidates; (ii) permutation-invariant: Reordering alternatives should not change the decision; (iii) option-scalable: Growing candidate sets should not require redefining the output space; (iv) cacheable: Request-independent computation over recurring alternatives should be reusable across requests. We introduce Jeva, a decision-native architecture that addresses these requirements jointly. A shared encoder independently represents the request and each option, while a compact decision stack refines only the request state against immutable option memory. Symmetric aggregation yields permutation-equivariant probabilities; shared scoring accommodates variable-size candidate sets. A separate coverage estimate distinguishes answer absence from candidate competition, enabling explicit null outcomes. Request-independent option representations and layer projections support reuse across newly assembled sets. These mechanisms unify Choice, Noul, and Score outputs. Across evaluations, Jeva combines strong typed-decision performance with near-perfect null detection and no decision flips under any tested permutations. It scales to thousands of candidates and substantially reduces latency through cross-request reuse without changing decisions.</summary>

    <title>Beyond the Verdict: Agentic Code Judging with Verifiable Feedback</title>
    <updated>2026-10-13T17:22:58Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18760v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18760v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Test-time scaling for large language models (LLMs) can involve generating multiple candidate solutions for selection or revising an earlier attempt. To guide selection and revision, we need a verifier that can estimate candidate correctness and provide evidence of failure. In competitive programming, however, official judging systems provide authoritative verdicts under finite submission budgets, without revealing failure explanations or failing inputs. To provide informative feedback without consuming official submissions, we formulate a task in which a model judges and diagnoses a candidate program using only the problem statement and source code, with generated counterexamples serving as checkable evidence. To evaluate this task, we build USACO-JUDGE from the USACO 2026 contests, using accepted and unaccepted programs written by human experts and multiple LLMs. We then train ARBITER, a 35B mixture-of-experts (MoE) agentic verifier, with reinforcement learning in a generic execution sandbox. Training raises counterexample success on incorrect programs from 40.61% to 62.67% and mean binary verdict accuracy on USACO-JUDGE from 71.41% to 87.41%, approaching frontier verification performance. Beyond verification, ARBITER outperforms baselines in both code selection and refinement. In an IOI 2026 case study, ARBITER-guided refinement raises GPT-OSS-120B's expected score above the gold-medal threshold under the official submission limit.</summary>

    <title>PreciseCoder: Faithful and Generalizable Debugging Beyond Unit-Test Rewards</title>
    <updated>2026-10-13T17:19:10Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18755v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18755v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Reinforcement learning (RL) from unit tests is the common recipe for post-training code models, but a unit test only asks whether the final program passes. We analyze what this unit-test-only reward teaches a model during debugging and find that, while it raises pass rates, it also teaches the model to edit more and to hallucinate bugs in code that is already correct. We introduce PreciseCoder, a training algorithm that augments the unit-test reward with a signal for semantically verified, localized edits, which correlates with smaller edits and higher pass rates. On 4B, 9B, and 27B models, PreciseCoder reduces the average number of edit lines from 7-15to 3 at a pass rate on par with unit-test-only training. Trained only on single-line bugs, PreciseCoder can generalize to repository-level program repair, where it resolves more issues with smaller patches. Its precision also transfers from weaker to stronger models: given the reasoning trace of a 9B PreciseCoder model, frontier models such as GPT-5.6 Sol and Qwen3.8-Max gain 4.6-12.4 points in edit precision with no additional training. Linguistic analysis of the thinking traces shows that our reward encourages the model to reason about individual lines, name the buggy ones, and form consistent bug hypotheses.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18745v1</id>
    <title>SolBehave: Evaluating the Behavioural Correctness of LLM-Generated Smart Contracts</title>
    <updated>2026-10-13T17:12:59Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18745v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18745v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Large language models increasingly generate Solidity smart contracts that, once deployed, can never be patched, making a single latent fault permanent and exploitable. Yet current evaluations mostly ask only whether generated code compiles. We introduce SolBehave, a benchmark for evaluating the correctness of model-generated contracts at scale, moving beyond ad hoc unit tests. Across 250 real, reproducible Ethereum contracts, we apply three complementary tests of behavioural fidelity: differential fuzzing, historical-transaction replay, and, as our core contribution, synthetic-transaction replay guided by a Dynamic Condition Response (DCR) graph that enumerates the space of legitimate function-call sequences. Differential fuzzing compares each generated function with the original on automatically generated inputs; historical replay compares the whole contract on the transactions it actually received on-chain; DCR-guided replay compares it on sequences of calls that follow its intended usage, including orderings that never occurred on-chain. We evaluate seven state-of-the-art open-weight models after one round of automated repair. Compilation success ranges from 26.4% to 92.7%, but under differential fuzzing only 31.4% of all generated function bodies that compile, pooled over models and samples, are equivalent to the original. Divergence at the contract level is the norm rather than the exception: for six of the seven models, between 13% and 31% of the generated contracts that compile diverge from the original under historical replay, and between 13% and 44% under DCR-guided replay; only Gemma-4-31B stays below 3% on both. Compilation is therefore a necessary condition for correctness and far from a sufficient one.</summary>

Ixabepilone will be administered over 1 hour on Days 1, 8, and 15 of a 28-day cycle. Dasatinib will be administered continuously starting on Day 1, Cycle 1 once daily (QD).

Three patients will be enrolled at dose level 0 and observed for dose-limiting toxicity (DLT) for 1 course of treatment.

Dose escalation or reduction will depend on the number of patients experiencing DLT as follows:

* If 0 of 3 patients experiences a DLT, then 3 additional patients will be enrolled at the next higher dose level.
* If 1 of 3 patients experiences a DLT, then 3 additional patients will be enrolled at that dose level.
* If 2 of 3 or 3 of 3 patients experience a DLT, then 3 patients will be enrolled at the next lower dose unless 6 patients have already been treated at that dose.
* If ≥2 of 6 patients experience a DLT at that dose level, then the MTD is considered to have been exceeded. At that point, 3 patients are treated at the next lower dose.
* If no more than 1 of the 6 patients experiences a DLT, then the dose level will be escalated 1 level.

Maximum-tolerated dose (MTD) is defined as the dose at which ≤1 of 6 patients experience DLT, and above which ≥2 of 6 patients experience DLT.

In the Phase II portion of the study, dasatinib and ixabepilone will be administered at the MTD determined during Phase I. Dasatinib will be started on Day 1, Cycle 1 and will be administered continuously once daily. Ixabepilone will be administered over 1 hour on Days 1, 8, and 15 of a 28-day cycle. A patient must meet each of the following criteria to be considered eligible for inclusion in this study:

1. Patient has the ability to understand and the willingness to sign a written informed consent including form according to institutional guidelines.
2. Patient has histologically-proven breast cancer.
3. Patient has locally recurrent or metastatic disease, measurable or non- measurable by RECIST criteria.
4. Patient has HER2-negative disease or disease that is refractory to HER2- directed therapy.
5. Patient is female or male ≥ 18 years of age.
6. Patient has(ECOG)performance status of ≤ 2.
7. Patient must have received at least 1 but no more than 2 prior chemotherapy regimens for locally recurrent or metastatic disease. Patients may have received neoadjuvant and/or adjuvant chemotherapy. These prior regimens can not have included ixabepilone or dasatinib. A line of chemotherapy will be defined as one or more agents used continuously or discontinuously (i.e., allowing a break or chemo holiday) without the addition of a new agent. Hormonal therapy will not be considered a line of therapy.
8. Prior chemotherapy must have been completed at least 3 weeks prior to study treatment start (6 weeks for nitrosoureas and mitomycin), and the patient must have recovered from all associated toxicities (except for alopecia and neuropathy grade 1 according to CTCAE, v3.0 classification).
9. Radiation therapy, immunotherapy, biologic therapy, and hormonal/endocrine therapy must have been completed at least 2 weeks prior to study treatment start. Any major surgery must have been completed at least 4 weeks prior to study treatment start.
10. Patient has adequate organ, metabolic and bone marrow function as follows:

    1. Total bilirubin ≤ 1.0 × institutional ULN
    2. AST, ALT ≤ 2.5 × institutional ULN
    3. Serum sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium, and phosphate ≥ institutional LLN. (Hypokalemia or hypomagnesemia must be corrected prior to dasatinib administration.)
    4. Serum creatinine \< 1.5 × institutional ULN
    5. Hematologic function: - ANC ≥ 1500/mm3. -Platelet count ≥ 100,000/mm3. - Hemoglobin ≥ 10.0 g/dL
    6. PT and PTT \< 1.5 x institutional ULN
11. Ability to take oral medication (dasatinib must be swallowed whole).
12. Concomitant medications:

    1. Patient agrees to discontinue St John's Wort at least 5 days prior to starting dasatinib therapy and while receiving dasatinib therapy.
    2. Patient agrees that IV bisphosphonates will be withheld for the first 8 weeks of dasatinib therapy due to risk of hypocalcemia.
    3. The use of CYP3A4 inducers, inhibitors, and substrates; medications that prolong QT interval; antacids; H2 blockers and proton pump inhibitors; and medications that inhibit platelet function and anticoagulation should be avoided during dasatinib therapy. These are restricted therapies that are permitted with caution when medically indicated.
13. Women of childbearing potential must have a negative serum or urine pregnancy test prior to the start of study treatment.
14. Patients of reproductive potential must agree to use and utilize an adequate method of contraception throughout treatment and for at least 4 weeks after study treatment is stopped.

Exclusion Criteria:

A patient who meets any of the following criteria will be considered not eligible for inclusion in this study:

1. Patient has had prior treatment with ixabepilone, dasatinib, or both.
2. Patient has had more than 2 prior lines of chemotherapy for locally recurrent or metastatic breast cancer. A line of chemotherapy will be defined as one or more agents used continuously or discontinuously (i.e., allowing a break or chemo holiday) without the addition of a new agent. Hormonal therapy will not be considered a line of therapy.
3. Patient has received a cumulative dose of \> 360 mg/m2 of doxorubicin or \> 600 mg/m2 of epirubicin.
4. Prior radiation must not have included ≥ 30% of major bone marrow containing areas (pelvis, lumbar spine).
5. Patients with CTC grade 2 or greater neuropathy (motor or sensory) at study entry.
6. Patient has evidence CNS or brain metastases, unless CNS or brain metastases have been treated and stable for \> 3 months.
7. Patient has psychiatric illness or social situation that would limit or prohibit compliance with study requirements.
8. Patient has an inability to take oral medication or inability to absorb oral medication.
9. Patient has had any invasive cancer other than the one being treated in this study within 3 years with the exception of surgically cured nonmelanoma skin cancer; in situ carcinoma of the cervix; in situ carcinoma of the breast.
10. Patient is receiving concurrent cancer therapy (chemotherapy, radiation therapy, immunotherapy, biologic therapy, or hormonal therapy for cancer).
11. Patient has other serious medical conditions as judged by the Principal Investigator.
12. Patient has a concurrent medical condition which may increase the risk of toxicity.
13. Patient has a pleural or pericardial effusion of any grade.
14. Patient has cardiac symptoms including any of the following:

    1. Uncontrolled angina, congestive heart failure or myocardial infarction within 6 months of study entry.
    2. Diagnosed congenital long QT syndrome.
    3. Any history of clinically significant ventricular arrhythmias (such as ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, or Torsades de pointes).
    4. Prolonged QTc on pre-entry ECG (\> 450 msec).
    5. Hypokalemia or hypomagnesemia if it cannot be corrected prior to dasatinib administration.
15. Patient has a history of significant bleeding disorder unrelated to cancer, including:

    1. Diagnosed congenital bleeding disorders (e.g., von Willebrand's disease).
    2. Diagnosed acquired bleeding disorder within one year (e.g., acquired anti-factor VIII antibodies).
    3. Ongoing or recent (≤ 3 months) significant GI bleeding.
16. Patient is taking any of the following concomitant medications at study entry:

    a. Category I drugs that are generally accepted to have a risk of causing Torsades de pointes including (Patients must discontinue drug 7 days prior to starting dasatinib.):
    * quinidine, procainamide, disopyramide.
    * amiodarone, sotalol, ibutilide, dofetilide.
    * erythromycin, clarithromycin.
    * chlorpromazine,haloperidol,mesoridazine, thioridazine,pimozide .
    * cisapride,bepridil, droperidol, methadone, arsenic, chloroquine, domperidone,halofantrine, levomethadyl, pentamidine,sparfloxacin, lidoflazine.
17. Patient has a history of allergic reactions attributed to compounds of similar chemical or biologic composition to ixabepilone or dasatinib. Ixabepilone is contraindicated in patients who have a known, prior, severe (CTC grade 3 or 4) history of hypersensitivity reaction to a drug formulated in Cremophor® EL (polyoxyethylated castor oil).
18. Patient has received any investigational agent or therapy within 30 days prior to study treatment start.
19. Patient is unwilling or unable to comply with study requirements.
20. Women who:

    1. are unwilling or unable to use an acceptable method to avoid pregnancy for the entire study period and for at least 4 weeks after cessation of study treatment, or
    2. have a positive pregnancy test at baseline, or
    3. are pregnant or breastfeeding.
21. The specific objectives are:

1. To evaluate the baseline nutritional status of cancer patients undergoing elective surgery
2. To evaluate the effectiveness of pre-operative ONS feeding on nutritional status in malnourished surgical cancer patients
3. To evaluate the effectiveness of an extended 3 months post-operative ONS feeding after discharge versus ONS feeding only post-operatively during hospital on nutritional status
4. To evaluate secondary outcomes of perioperative feeding such as sleep quality, post-operative complications and length of hospital stay

Study Design: This is a randomised-controlled-open label-parallel group(s)-trial which will be conducted on malnourished cancer patients undergoing elective surgery.

Approximately 5% of the world's population carries trait genes for haemoglobin disorders, mainly, sickle-cell disease and thalassaemia. The incidence of sickle cell disease varies according to different geographical locations. Persons with SCD experience both acute and chronic pain. it is important that nonpharmacological therapies be investigated and used as complements to pharmacological therapies to address and treat both acute and chronic pain for those with SCD. An educational program involving parents with children with SCD can help parents use nonpharmacological methods for their children in reducing pain. The training program allows parents to develop their knowledge of the SCD and the importance of non-pharmacological methods, and may provide parents with the opportunity to develop preventive attitudes towards reducing pain crises. The research has two purposes. The first is to identify the non-pharmacological approaches that parents use to help their children with sickle cell disease in Turkey, Chad. Second, to determine the effectiveness of non-pharmacological approaches given to parents in Turkey, Chad.

Method: This study is an experimental research method using a quasi-experimental design. This study used a pretest and posttest, with a design that is used is the two group pretest-posttest design. The study was conducted on the parents of children with sickle cell disease diagnosed and followed up in the Pediatric Hematology Oncology polyclinics of two hospitals in Chad in Central Africa between September 2015 and February 2016. The study found in April 2016 and July 2016 between Turkey's southern Antalya and Mersin two university hospital outpatient Children's pediatric hematology oncology has made clinic on sickle cell disease diagnosed and monitored the children's parents. The parents were selected using eligibility criteria and the study was performed in three steps (Pre-intervention testing session, education session, and post-intervention testing session). In the first step, "Information Form", "Parents' Experience of Nonpharmacological Methods Questionnaire", and "Nonpharmacological Approaches Used by Parents for Their Children and Knowledge of Parents about Nonpharmacological Approaches Questionnaire" questionnaires were applied to parents. In the second step an individual education was conducted by the researcher using the education book. In the third step, the questionnaire were reapplied after 3 weeks.","detailedDescription":"In this study, nonpharmacological approaches used by parents of sickle cell anemia patients were determined. The purpose of this randomized clinical trial is to conduct a randomized trial testing the impact of the collaborative palliative and oncology care model or standard oncology care models among patients with poor prognosis metastatic breast cancer. Participants assigned to the intervention arm will participate in a series of structured palliative care visits, following tailored clinical practice guidelines previously developed for patients with metastatic breast cancer.","detailedDescription":"This research study tests whether or not the earlier introduction of a team of clinicians that specialize in the lessening (palliation) of symptoms and addressing quality of life concerns may improve the end-of-life care, quality of life, and mood of women with poor prognosis metastatic breast cancer.

Palliative care is a specific type of medical care given to patients to improve their pain and other symptoms like fatigue, and to support patients and their families as they cope with their illness. Palliative care includes physicians and advanced practice nurses who have been specifically trained in how to help patients with serious illness.

Increasingly, the role of palliative care has been shown to benefit patients when introduced early in the disease trajectory. For example, in patients with metastatic (or spread) lung cancer, early involvement of palliative care improves patients' quality of life and mood.
